summary: Proposes using DTLS to protect DNS queries and responses from passive listeners and some active attacks, while keeping latency low. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary:
DNS over DTLS encrypts DNS queries and replies so that anyone watching the network between the client and the server cannot read them or change them. It uses UDP rather than TCP, which keeps the delay low.

The RFC calls this an experimental backup to DNS over TLS, and it is meant for deployments that want privacy without the extra round trips that a TCP connection costs.

subtitle: Wrapping DNS queries in DTLS over UDP port 853 so eavesdroppers cannot read them, as an experimental backup to DNS over TLS.

tldr.problem: DNS queries and responses normally travel unencrypted, so anything on the path can learn which names a host looks up and can tamper with the answers.
tldr.mechanism: DNS over DTLS carries the DNS exchange inside Datagram Transport Layer Security over UDP port 853. That encrypts the messages and authenticates the server, and it avoids the head-of-line blocking that TCP suffers from.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is an experimental backup to DNS over TLS. Clients that want strict privacy must also implement DNS over TLS, because a DTLS record that does not fit the path MTU leads to a truncated answer.

facts.label: DTLS overhead per message
facts.value: At least 13 octets of header, plus cipher and authentication overhead

facts.label: Assumed IP MTU when it is unknown
How often to probe for the service
facts.value: Never more often than every 15 minutes, and not more often than every 24 hours

today: RFC 8094 is an Experimental document and has not been obsoleted. The RFC says it was written as a backup in case the TLS-based approach of RFC 7858 has problems when deployed, and that at the time of writing RFC 7858 was expected to be what would be deployed.

sections.title: Why Encrypt DNS
sections.content:
The Domain Name System is specified in RFC 1034 and RFC 1035. DNS queries and responses are normally exchanged unencrypted, so they are vulnerable to eavesdropping. Eavesdropping can result in an unwanted party learning which domain a host wishes to access, which is a privacy leak. The DNS privacy problem is discussed further in RFC 7626.

This document defines DNS over DTLS, which provides confidential DNS communication between stub resolvers and recursive resolvers, between stub resolvers and forwarders, and between forwarders and recursive resolvers. The largest gain in privacy comes from protecting the link between the DNS client, which is the end user's machine, and its caching resolver. The document does not change the format of DNS messages.

Two reasons are given for proposing DTLS rather than only TLS. TCP suffers from network head-of-line blocking, where the loss of a packet holds up all other TCP segments until the lost packet is retransmitted; DNS over DTLS uses UDP and so does not suffer from it. And DTLS session resumption consumes one round trip, whereas TLS session resumption can start only after the TCP handshake is complete, although with TCP Fast Open an implementation can reach the same efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary DNS traffic can be read by anyone on the path between the client and the server. Putting DTLS around it hides the queries and stops anyone changing the answers, and it keeps the delay low because it does not wait for a TCP connection first.

sections.title: DNS over DTLS and DNS over TLS
sections.content:
DNS queries can be sent over UDP or TCP, but the scope of this document is only UDP. DNS over TCP can be protected with TLS as described in RFC 7858.

DNS over DTLS alone cannot give privacy in every circumstance. The problem arises when the DTLS record size is larger than the path MTU, the largest packet that fits on the path. In that situation the DNS server responds with a truncated response. For that reason, DNS clients and servers that implement DNS over DTLS must also implement DNS over TLS, so that they can still give privacy to clients that ask for strict privacy.

DNSSEC, the DNS Security Extensions, provide object integrity of DNS resource records, which lets an end user or its resolver verify that a response is legitimate. DNSSEC does not provide privacy for requests or responses. DNS over DTLS works together with DNSSEC but does not replace the need for it.

The RFC also notes that this DTLS solution was considered by the working group as an option to use in case the TLS-based approach turns out to have issues when deployed. At the time of writing it was expected that RFC 7858 would be deployed, so this specification is mainly intended as a backup.
sections.plainLanguage: DTLS is the backup plan, not the main plan. The TLS version was expected to be what people would deploy, so this RFC exists for the case where the TLS version turns out to have problems.

sections.title: Starting, Using and Ending a Session
sections.content:
By default, DNS over DTLS must run over standard UDP port 853, unless the server and its clients have agreed on another port. Such a port must not be port 53, but it may come from the first-come, first-served range of User Ports, 1024 to 49151. Using something other than port 53 avoids complications in choosing whether to use DTLS and reduces the risk of downgrade attacks.

A client finds out whether the server offers DNS over DTLS by sending a DTLS ClientHello to port 853. A server that does not support DNS over DTLS will not answer it. If nothing comes back and the client has no better estimate of the round-trip time, it should retransmit the ClientHello and should stop trying after 15 seconds. The client may repeat that procedure later to discover whether the service has become available, but such probing should not be done more frequently than every 24 hours and must not be done more frequently than every 15 minutes. Clients and servers must not use port 853 to carry cleartext DNS messages, and a client must not send cleartext DNS messages on a port used for DNS over DTLS, for example after a failed handshake, because mixing protected and unprotected data has significant security issues.

The client then runs the DTLS handshake, and once negotiation completes the connection is encrypted and protected from eavesdropping. To protect against attackers pretending to be the server, the client must use the authentication mechanisms of the DTLS profile for DNS. Within one session, DNS messages are written to the DTLS implementation as ordinary application data, and a single session can carry many requests and responses.

To avoid unintentional server overload, clients must keep the number of concurrent sessions to any one server low, and one session per client and server is recommended. Servers may limit concurrent sessions per client address or subnet. While traffic is quiet the client may send DTLS heartbeats, which keep the cryptographic state alive and keep firewall and NAT bindings open. A session ends when the server sends a DTLS fatal alert after an idle period, which tells the client to establish a new cryptographic context before sending anything else.
sections.plainLanguage: The client tests for support by knocking on port 853, then sets up an encrypted session and reuses it for many queries. Servers close an idle session by sending an alert, and the client then knows it must handshake again before sending more.

sections.title: Reducing the Cost of the Handshake
sections.content:
Latency matters for DNS, so the RFC looks for ways to cut both the number of round trips and the size of the handshake. The size of the certificate in the ServerHello can be several kilobytes, so clients and servers can use raw public keys or the Cached Information Extension. The cached information extension avoids sending the server's certificate and chain when the client already has that information from a previous handshake. TLS False Start can reduce round trips by letting the second flight of messages also carry the encrypted DNS query.

It is highly advantageous to avoid server-side DTLS state and to reduce the number of new sessions, which is what session resumption without server-side state achieves. It also removes a round trip for later queries, because the session does not have to be established again. If DTLS 1.3 is used it provides critical latency improvements for connection establishment over DTLS 1.2.

Because responses within a session can arrive out of order, clients must match responses to outstanding queries on the same connection using the DNS Message ID, and if the response carries a question section they must also match the QNAME, QCLASS and QTYPE fields. Failing to match responses properly can have serious consequences for interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the cost is in the first handshake, so the RFC suggests ways to make it smaller and to avoid repeating it. Because replies can arrive out of order, the client uses the ID in the query to work out which reply belongs to which question.

sections.title: Path MTU, Anycast and Usage
sections.content:
Compared with normal DNS, DTLS adds at least 13 octets of header, plus cipher and authentication overhead, to every query and every response, which reduces the size of the DNS payload that can be carried. Clients and servers must support the EDNS0 option so that the client can say the largest DNS response it can reassemble. If the client does set that option, the maximum DNS response size of 512 bytes plus DTLS overhead stays within the path MTU. If the path MTU is not known, an IP MTU of 1280 bytes should be assumed.

The server must make sure the response fits the path MTU, so each DTLS record must fit within a single datagram. The path MTU must be at least the DNS response size plus 13 octets of DTLS overhead plus the padding size plus the authentication overhead of the negotiated cipher suite plus block padding. If the response would be larger, the server must send a shorter response and set the TC, truncated, bit. A client that wants the whole answer and receives a truncated one must, for strict privacy, send a new request for the same record over an encrypted transport such as DNS over TLS. A client using opportunistic privacy should try for the best case but may fall back to clear text to get an answer.

DNS servers are often configured with anycast addresses. While the network is stable, packets sent to an anycast address reach the same server that holds the cryptographic context from the handshake. When routing changes, a packet can reach a server without that context, so clients must always be ready to start a new handshake. Servers should answer such a packet with a DTLS fatal alert, and the client should keep retransmitting and start session resumption at the same time, in case the alert was spoofed.

The RFC then gives the order of preference for DNS usage: encrypted DNS messages with an authenticated server, then encrypted DNS messages with an unauthenticated server, and finally plaintext DNS messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption makes every packet bigger, so the server has to check that the answer still fits on the path. If it does not, the answer is shortened and marked as truncated, and a client that insists on the full answer has to ask again over another encrypted channel.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The interaction between a DNS client and a DNS server requires DTLS with a ciphersuite that offers confidentiality protection, and the guidance on avoiding attacks on DTLS must be followed. The client should use the TLS Certificate Status Request extension, commonly called OCSP stapling, to check the revocation status of the server's public key certificate. Keeping track of which servers are known to support DTLS also lets clients detect downgrade attacks.

To interfere with DNS over DTLS, an attacker might send an ICMP message towards the client or the server. Such messages cannot be authenticated, so all ICMP errors should be treated as soft errors. If a query was sent over DTLS, the matching response must only be accepted if it arrives over the same DTLS connection, which mitigates the attacks described in RFC 5452.

A malicious client might try to perform a high number of DTLS handshakes with a server. Because clients are not uniquely identified by the protocol and can be hidden behind address sharing or temporary addresses, a server needs to limit the impact, for example by rate limiting handshakes from a given subnet.
sections.plainLanguage: The server has to be checked as well as the traffic hidden. A reply is only believed if it arrives over the same encrypted connection that carried the question, and a server needs to limit how many handshakes it accepts from one network.
